issue_context.title: `gh repo garden` does not reset the terminal to proper state
issue_context.body:
### Describe the bug

When I run `gh repo garden` and quit using 'ctrl-c' my cursor stays hidden.
When I run `gh repo garden` and quit using 'q' I am still in noecho mode (I don't see the characters I type).

gh version: v1.0.0
Terminal: Konsole 20.08.1
`$TERM`: xterm-256color

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. type `gh repo garden`
2. press 'ctrl-c'
3. the cursor is now not visible anymore

or 

1. type `gh repo garden`
2. press 'q'
3. type any text
4. the text is not shown in the terminal

### Relevant

Termios has an option to get the current state of terminal settings and save them.
After the execution of the program it can reset the terminal to its old state.
See this [python example](https://docs.python.org/3/library/termios.html#example).

I think the cursor visibility is not included in this, so that should be done separately
comments:
the code is trying to reset but clearly I didn't do it correctly or portably -- i know i do get my cursor back when exiting with `q` in my environment (gnome-terminal, fish). i'll have to audit the terminal reset code across platforms.

it also might be time to give up and pull in one of the third party libraries that can manage terminal state for me.
it does give my cursor back when exiting with `q`; it just doesn't show the text I type anymore. Hiding the cursor only happens when I quit with ctrl-c

I found the answer to a problem with similar symptoms. I'll include it here for someone who finds this page looking for an answer, as I did.

In my case, the cursor didn't move, or show my typing onscreen.
However, it actually executed the command (if I pressed Enter), even though it looked like I didn't type anything in!

The solution was to type reset < Enter >

Turns out it can be an issue for any shell program (cmd, git bash, etc), not necessarily just a Git Bash issue.
It looks like Ctrl-C or Ctrl-Z can occasionally result in the terminal not echoing commands to the screen, depending on what process was running at the time it was killed.

reset restores it.

I suppose this is actually 2 different issues:
The hidden cursor is just because ctrl-c is not caught, or the reset is not done in the ctrl-c handling.
The noecho issue is something that only happens in a regular exit.

I found out that the noecho issue appears on bash, csh and ksh, but not on fish and zsh
Okay please show the photocopy issue I will try to understand native of problem

Your description of the noecho problem is accurate: I can type the characters and they are used, but they don't actually show up on the screen (similar to when you're entering a password with getpass).
I just wanted to add more information for clarification.
The problem is caused because https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/72eeae9d1dc4af1fd40e3271ad17125e8c1b8237/pkg/cmd/repo/garden/garden.go#L209 isn't undone when exiting the program.

The cursor problem is caused because https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/72eeae9d1dc4af1fd40e3271ad17125e8c1b8237/pkg/cmd/repo/garden/garden.go#L293 is only executed at a normal exit, and not when exiting with ctrl-c.
It doesn't surprise me that it is more common, but it is possible to add a SIGINT handler to restore the proper state.

I'm actually surprosed that the noecho problem does not occur when I close with ctrl-c. The code looks like it should occur on every exit. Maybe bash has a built-in reset for terminal settings when you use ctrl-c?

I've managed to fix the noecho problem in #2072 

The hidden cursor problem still remains.

review_comments: IMO this would be good to extract into normal function. This may be a silly question but from a Go perspective, Is there a reason it should be defined inline like this?

@samcoe Good question! This is an example of using a closure like in JavaScript. The references to `opts`, `out`, and `oldTTYSettings` are provided to us by the closure.

If the `walkAway()` function was defined top-level, we could invoke it, but we would have to pass all the references as arguments. It wouldn't be a huge deal, but in this case, a closure is convenient and we're not planning to call `walkAway()` from anywhere else, so I'm fine with this approach.
